prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

and acceptance criteria shall be formulated in accordance with design requirements and site conditions. 1.1.5 Maintenance Key Points 1. Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Table 1.2-1 Recommended Curb Radius Values | Road class | Recommended curb radius (m) | |---|---:| | Main and secondary arterial roads | 5–10 | | Branch roads | 5–8 | Note: For exclusive right-turn lanes with traffic islands, the recommended curb radius is 8–10 m. Figure 1.2-1 Reducing Road Curb Radius B. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority. justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple users: a wide motor-vehicle carriageway is paired with sidewalks or side paths on both sides, indicating a relatively balanced distribution of corridor space for all road users.

Continuous tree-lined verges and separated side paths on both sides suggest that non-motorized users are not entirely excluded from the corridor, which supports equity in access to the street environment.

Accessibility appears only moderate because no curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free details are visible in the image, so inclusive access cannot be fully confirmed from this scene.
safety: The roadway is very wide and straight with long sightlines, allowing drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians to see far ahead, which generally improves conflict anticipation.
Streetlights are visible along the corridor, supporting basic nighttime visibility and perceived security for all road users.

Safety is reduced by the apparent absence of visible crosswalks, refuge islands, traffic calming, or intersection controls in this view; on such a broad road, crossing could be difficult if speeds are high.
livability: The corridor is lined with abundant mature trees and landscaped edges, creating a park-like setting that supports a pleasant everyday environment.
Low visible traffic volumes and the absence of roadside clutter, parked cars, or heavy commercial loading make the street feel calm and less stressful.
Livability is limited by the lack of visible active frontages, shops, seating, bus stops, or social destinations, so the space appears more scenic than socially vibrant.
sustainability: Extensive tree cover on both sides provides meaningful green infrastructure, which supports shade, air-quality benefits, and ecological value.
The presence of continuous side paths separated from the main carriageway can support walking and potentially cycling, helping reduce dependence on private cars.
Landscaped verges and planted medians or edge strips indicate a greener street design than a fully paved corridor, although no explicit stormwater features are visible.
aesthetics: The double rows of trees create strong visual order and rhythm along the corridor, giving the street a coherent and attractive composition.
The pavement, curbs, planting beds, and lighting poles appear clean and well maintained, which enhances visual quality.
Open views toward distant hills combined with lush greenery produce a scenic boulevard character with high visual appeal.
comfort: Large roadside trees provide substantial shade potential along the sidewalks or side paths, improving thermal comfort for people outside vehicles.
The road surface appears smooth and newly paved, which supports physical comfort for drivers and likely for cyclists if they use the side paths.
Psychological comfort is helped by the quiet, uncrowded setting and generous spatial separation between the carriageway and the landscaped pedestrian realm.
walkability: Sidewalks or shared side paths appear continuous on both sides of the road, which supports basic route continuity for walking.
Tree-lined edges and landscaped buffers make walking more pleasant than on an exposed arterial, improving the attractiveness of the route.

Walkability is constrained because no visible crosswalks, curb ramps, pedestrian signals, benches, or active destinations are present in this view, so crossing convenience and pedestrian support remain limited.

 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)

All Road Users; All Social Groups

Justice
- Equity

- Accessibility
Safety
Livability

- Psychological Comfort

Selected Indicators:

 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Data were collected for six hours (8–10 h, 11–13 h, and 16–18 h) on three weekdays in September through December 2018 at each location. The video recording times were selected based on peak expected combined volumes of pedestrians, bicycles, and motor vehicles, with a target of observing 200 pedestrian crossings with interactions from each location. Video data were manually reviewed to identify potential interactions of crossing pedestrians with motor vehicles or bicycles, defined using a conservative threshold of approximately 5 s passing time. Passing time (sometimes referred to as post encroachment time) is the time gap between when the first road user exits the point at which their paths intersect and when the second road user enters it. Although no conflict indicator completely captures risk, passing time is the most popular measure for studies of crossing pedestrians and other road users on transverse trajectories (Mahmud et al., 2017). A total of 4428 potential pedestrian interactions were identified: 3176 (72%) with motor vehicles and 1252 (28%) with bicycles. Due to the time cost of coding interactions, a random sample of 50 pedestrian crossings with interactions was selected from each location (except for the one low-volume location that had only 36), giving 536 crossings for further analysis. These 536 crossings were then stratified on combinations of passing time (<2, 2–3, 3–4 s) and interacting road user type (bicycles, motor vehicles, or both), which were both manually coded (see Table 1). Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Table 1.2-1 Recommended Curb Radius Values | Road class | Recommended curb radius (m) | |---|---:| | Main and secondary arterial roads | 5–10 | | Branch roads | 5–8 | Note: For exclusive right-turn lanes with traffic islands, the recommended curb radius is 8–10 m. Figure 1.2-1 Reducing Road Curb Radius B. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority.
